_comment: Shared adversarial-command corpus for the two independent Bash classifiers. cmdparse.sh (this repo, bash) segments a command for the guards that judge it; auto-approve-readonly.py (~/server/.claude/hooks, python) decides whether a command is read-only enough to auto-approve. They are deliberately separate implementations — cmdparse.sh's header records why it is bash and not python: it is on the hot path of every Bash call, and a missing interpreter would be a new fail-open surface. What they must NOT do is diverge on which strings are dangerous, and nothing checked that until this file existed. Each side asserts the field it owns: `cmdparse` here, `readonly` in the server repo's test_command_vectors.py. Every value below was measured against both implementations on 2026-08-17, not assumed. Adding a vector means running both sides and recording what they actually do — if they disagree, that is the finding this corpus exists to surface.

fields.readonly: auto-approve-readonly.py classify() must return a reason when true, and None when false
fields.cmdparse: cmdparse.sh --json contract: status, plus top-level segments after trimming and dropping empties
fields.cmdparse.seps: optional: the separator that terminated each segment, in order (&& || ; | & newline eof). Pinned where the separator IS the verdict, as for a trailing `&`

vectors.name: newline separates two commands
vectors.why: shlex and a flattening regex both treat a newline as whitespace and merge the pair, which is the documented bypass class both implementations were fixed for

vectors.name: newline hides a remote reboot
vectors.why: same split, but the tail is an ssh payload the remote-approval path would otherwise never see

vectors.name: semicolon control
vectors.why: the newline forms must agree with the separator every implementation already handled

vectors.name: && with no surrounding spaces
vectors.why: a splitter keying on ' && ' rather than the operator misses this

vectors.name: lone & backgrounds and starts a new command
vectors.why: a splitter that glues the tail onto the previous segment lets 'rm -rf /' inherit ls's approval, since only the segment prefix is matched

vectors.name: command substitution
vectors.why: the payload never appears as a top-level segment, so it must be refused on the substitution itself rather than on its contents

vectors.name: unbalanced quote is unreadable, not empty
vectors.why: an unparseable command must fail closed; treating it as zero segments reads as nothing to object to

vectors.name: a heredoc body is data, not a command
vectors.why: the opposite error to the newline case — splitting the body on newlines turns 'rm -rf /' into a phantom command and prompts on ordinary gh pr create --body-file - <<EOF

vectors.name: trailing backslash continues onto an unseen line
vectors.why: whatever follows the continuation is not in the string being judged

vectors.name: redirect to a real file is a write
read-only pipeline
vectors.why: controls: over-blocking is the failure mode a corpus of only-dangerous vectors cannot catch

vectors.name: a trailing ampersand still reads as backgrounding
vectors.why: the trailing-separator collapse used to rewrite the surviving segment sep to `eof`, so `ls &` parsed as a bare `ls` and the classifier needed a textual endswith ampersand rule to refuse it (DanielH2018/server#2261). The segments alone cannot pin this — both sides return ["ls"] — so the sep is what this vector asserts
